content: The text provided appears to be a list of references from various studies and articles related to infant feeding practices, nutrition, and their effects on health outcomes. 1. Pluymen LPM, Wijga AH, Gehring U, Koppelman GH, Smit HA, van Rossem L conducted a study in the Netherlands examining the early introduction of complementary foods and its association with childhood overweight in both breastfed and formula-fed infants. This research was part of the PIAMA birth cohort study and was published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2018. 2. Wang F, Liu H, Wan Y, Li J, Chen Y, Zheng J, and colleagues investigated the age of complementary food introduction and its relationship with anemia risk in children aged 4-6 years. This prospective birth cohort study was conducted in China and published in Scientific Reports. 3. Wright CM, Parkinson KN, and Drewett RF explored the reasons why some infants are weaned early. Their findings were based on data from a prospective population-based cohort study and were published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2004. 4. Rossem Lv, Kiefte-de Jong JC, Looman CWN, Jaddoe VWV, Hofman A, and Hokken-Koelega ACS analyzed weight changes before and after the introduction of solid foods. Their longitudinal birth cohort study results were published in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2013. 5. Mondal SK, Gupta PG, Gupta DN, Ghosh S, Sikder SN, and Rajendran K examined the occurrence of diarrheal diseases in relation to infant feeding practices in a rural community in West Bengal, India. Their findings were published in Acta Paediatrica in 1996. 6. Wen LM, Baur LA, Rissel C, Xu H, and Simpson JM identified correlates of body mass index, overweight, and obesity in children aged 2 years. Their findings were derived from the Healthy Beginnings Trial and published in Obesity (Silver Spring) in 2014. 7. Libuda L, Hilbig A, Berber-Al-Tawil S, Kalhoff H, and Kersting M studied the association between full breastfeeding, the timing of complementary food introduction, and iron status in infancy in Germany. Their secondary analysis of a randomized trial was published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2018. 8. Gooze RA, Anderson SE, and Whitaker RC examined the prevalence of obesity in 5-year-old children in the United States. Their findings were published in the Journal of Pediatrics in 2011. 9. Isherwood R, Dimond C, and Longhurst S investigated breastfeeding and weaning practices in relation to the nutritional status of children under 5 years in North Bangladesh. Their study was published in the Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 1988. 10. Zutavern A, Brockow I, Schaaf B, Bolte G, von Berg A, and Diez U explored the timing of solid food introduction and its relationship with atopic dermatitis and atopic sensitization. Their prospective birth cohort study results were published in Pediatrics in 2006. 11. Zutavern A, Brockow I, Schaaf B, von Berg A, Diez U, and Borte M examined the timing of solid food introduction in relation to eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food and inhalant sensitization at age 6 years. Their findings were part of the LISA birth cohort study and published in Pediatrics in 2008. 12. Khadivzadeh T and Parsai S studied the effects of exclusive breastfeeding and complementary feeding on infant growth and morbidity. Their findings were published in the Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal in 2004. 13. Barton SJ, Howard PK, and Rayens MK analyzed the effects of infant feeding decisions on infant growth. Their study was published in the Journal for Specialists in Pediatric Nursing in 2002. 14. Grunwaldt E, Bates T, and Guthrie Jr D investigated the onset of sleeping through the night in infancy and its relationship to the introduction of solid foods, birth weight, and family position. Their findings were published in Pediatrics in 1960. 15. Quandt SA studied the effect of beikost (complementary foods) on the diet of breastfed infants. The research was published in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association in 1984. 16. Wolman PG examined feeding practices in infancy and the prevalence of obesity in preschool children. The study was published in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association in 1984. 17. Winkelstein ML explored overfeeding in infancy and the early introduction of solid foods. The findings were published in Pediatric Nursing in 1984. 18. Kalies H, Heinrich J, Borte N, Schaaf B, von Berg A, and von Kries R studied the effect of breastfeeding on weight gain in infants. Their birth cohort study results were published in the European Journal of Medical Research in 2005. 19. Tufa EG, Dake SK, Bekru ET, Tekle HA, Bobe TM, and Angore BN investigated the magnitude of wasting and underweight among children aged 6-59 months in Sodo Zuria District, South Ethiopia. Their community-based cross-sectional study was published in BMC Research Notes in 2018. 20. Vehapoglu A, Goknar N, Turel O, Torun E, and Ozgurhan G analyzed risk factors for childhood obesity, including birth weight, type of delivery, and maternal overweight. Their findings were published in the World Journal of Pediatrics in 2017. 21. Forsyth JS, Ogston SA, Clark A, Florey CD, and Howie PW examined the relationship between the early introduction of solid food to infants and their weight and illnesses during the first two years of life. Their study was published in BMJ in 1993. 22. Yang W, Li X, Li Y, Zhang S, Liu L, and Wang X studied anemia, malnutrition, and their correlations with socio-demographic characteristics and feeding practices among infants aged 0-18 months in rural areas of Shaanxi Province, China. Their cross-sectional study was published in BMC Public Health in 2012. 23. De Beer M, Vrijkotte TGM, Fall CHD, Van Eijsden M, Osmond C, and Gemke RJBJ investigated associations of infant feeding and timing of weight gain and linear growth during early life with childhood blood pressure. Their findings were published in PLoS ONE in 2016. 24. Gisht O, Jaddoe VW, Duijts L, Franco OH, Hofman A, and Ikram MK studied the influence of breastfeeding on retinal vessel calibers in school-age children. Their findings were part of the Generation R Study and published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016. 25. Gisht O, Gaillard R, Durmuş B, Hofman A, Duijts L, and Franco OH examined infant diet and metabolic outcomes in school-age children. Their findings were part of the Generation R Study and published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2014. 26. Penick EC, Nickel EJ, Chhibber S, Knop J, and colleagues explored the relationship between breastfeeding and alcoholism, proposing the Trotter hypothesis. Their study was published in the American Journal of Psychiatry in 1999. 27. Salmenperä L, Perheentupa J, and Siimes MA found that exclusively breastfed healthy infants grow slower than reference infants. Their study was published in Pediatric Research in 1985. 28. Størdal K, Lundeby KM, Brantsæter AL, Haugen M, Nakstad B, and Lund-Blix NA examined breastfeeding and infant hospitalization for infections. Their large cohort and sibling analysis were published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2017. 29. Sit C, Yeung DL, He MZ, and Anderson GH studied the growth and feeding patterns of 9to 12-month-old Chinese Canadian infants. Their findings were published in Nutrition Research in 2001. 30. Yuan WL, Lange C, Schwartz C, Martin C, Chabanet C, and de Lauzon-Guillain B investigated infant dietary exposures to sweetness and fattiness during the first year of life and their association with feeding practices. Their study was published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2016. 31. Gebreweld A, Ali N, Ali R, and Fisha T examined the prevalence of anemia and its associated factors among children under five years of age attending Guguf Health Center in South Wollo, Ethiopia. Their findings were published in PLoS ONE in 2019. 32. Elalfy MS, Hamdy AM, Maksoud SS, and Megeed RI studied the pattern of milk feeding and family size as risk factors for iron deficiency anemia among poor Egyptian infants aged 6 to 24 months. Their findings were published in Nutrition Research in 2012. 33. Ekelund L, Gloppen I, Øien T, and Simpson MR examined the duration of breastfeeding, age at complementary food introduction, and allergy-related diseases. Their prospective cohort study was published in the International Breastfeeding Journal in 2021. 34. Differding MK, Doyon M, Bouchard L, Perron P, Guérin R, and Asselin C explored the interaction between the timing of complementary feeding and breastfeeding duration in determining early childhood gut microbiota composition and BMI. Their study was published in Pediatric Obesity in 2020. 35. Differding MK, Benjamin-Neelon SE, Hoyo C, Østbye T, and Mueller NT studied the association between the timing of complementary feeding and gut microbiota diversity, composition, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations during the first year of life. Their findings were published in BMC Microbiology in 2020. 36. Dhami MV, Ogbo FA, Osuagwu UL, Ugboma Z, and Agho KE examined stunting and severe stunting among infants in India, focusing on the role of delayed complementary food introduction and community and household factors. Their study was published in Global Health Action in 2019. 37. Durmuş B, Heppe DHM, Gisht O, Manniesing R, Abrahamsse-Berkveld M, and van der Beek EM studied general and abdominal fat outcomes in school-age children associated with infant breastfeeding patterns. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2014. 38. Tessama M, Belachew T, and Ersino G investigated feeding patterns and stunting during early childhood in rural communities of Sidama, South Ethiopia. Their study was published in the Pan African Medical Journal. 39. Malako BG, Teshome MS, and Belachew T examined anemia and associated factors among children aged 6-23 months in Damot Sore District, Wolaita Zone, South Ethiopia. Their findings were published in BMC Hematology in 2018. 40. Kleynhans IC, MacIntyre UE, and Albertse EC studied stunting among young black children and the socio-economic and health status of their mothers/caregivers in poor areas of rural Limpopo and urban Gauteng, South Africa. Their findings were part of the NutriGro Study and published in the South African Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2006. 41. Kamudoni P, Maleta K, Shi Z, and Holmboe-Ottesen G found that exclusive breastfeeding duration during the first six months of life is positively associated with length-for-age among infants aged 6-12 months in Mangochi District, Malawi. Their study was published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015. 42. Jeana H, Ju-Young C, Sue S, and Sohee OH studied the association between breastfeeding, red meat intake, and iron status in healthy Korean weaning-age infants. Their findings were published in the Journal of Korean Medical Science in 2017. 43. Gingras V, Aris IM, Rifas-Shiman SL, Switkowski KM, Oken E, and Hivert MF examined the associations of the timing of complementary feeding introduction with adiposity throughout childhood and adolescence. Their study was published in Circulation. 44. Fauzia RA, Badruddin IA, and Setiawati F investigated the association between early childhood caries and feeding patterns in 3to 5-year-old children in Grogol Utara, South Jakarta. Their findings were published in Pesquisa Brasileira em Odontopediatria e Clínica Integrada in 2020. 45. Chuang CH, Hsieh WS, Chen YC, Chang PJ, Hurng BS, and Lin SJ studied infant feeding practices and physician-diagnosed atopic dermatitis in Taiwan. Their prospective cohort study was published in Pediatric Allergy and Immunology in 2011. 46. Kanoa BJ, Zabut BM, and Harried AT compared the nutritional status and nutritional history of preschool-aged children in Gaza Strip. Their cross-sectional study was published in the Pakistan Journal of Nutrition in 2011. 47. Hay G, Johnston C, Whitelaw A, Trygg K, and Refsum H examined folate and cobalamin status in relation to breastfeeding and weaning in healthy infants. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2008. 48. Sirkka O, Hof MH, Vrijkotte T, Abrahamsse-Berkveld M, Halberstadt J, and Seidell JC studied feeding patterns and BMI trajectories during infancy in a multi-ethnic, prospective birth cohort. Their findings were published in BMC Pediatrics in 2021. 49. Deisher RW and Goers SS conducted a study on the early and later introduction of solids into the infant diet. Their findings were published in the Journal of Pediatrics in 1954. 50. Shamim S, Naz F, Jamalvi SW, and Ali SS examined the effect of the weaning period on the nutritional status of children. Their study was published in the Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan in 2006. 51. Zutavern A, von Mutius E, Harris J, Mills P, Moffatt S, and White C studied the introduction of solids in relation to asthma and eczema. Their findings were published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2004. 52. Salah RW, Hasab AAH, El-Nimr NA, and Tayel DI examined the prevalence and predictors of iron deficiency anemia among rural infants in Nablus Governorate. Their findings were published in the Journal of Research in Health Sciences in 2018. 53. Hodgson SV studied early infant feeding and weight gain. Their findings were published in the Journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners in 1978. 54. Zheng JS, Liu H, Zhao YM, Li J, Chen Y, and Zhu S examined complementary feeding and childhood adiposity in preschool-aged children in a large Chinese cohort. Their findings were published in the Journal of Pediatrics. 55. Grimshaw KEC, Maskell J, Oliver EM, Morris RCG, Foote KD, and Clare Mills EN studied the introduction of complementary foods and its relationship to food allergy. Their findings were published in Pediatrics in 2013. 56. Wilson AC, Forsyth JS, Greene SA, Irvine L, Hau C, and Howie PW examined the relationship between infant diet and childhood health in a seven-year follow-up of a cohort of children from the Dundee Infant Feeding Study. Their findings were published in BMJ in 1998. 57. Baird J, Poole J, Robinson S, Marriott L, Godfrey K, and Cooper C studied milk feeding and dietary patterns as predictors of weight and fat gains in infancy. Their findings were published in Paediatric and Perinatal Epidemiology in 2008. 58. Sina E, Buck C, Jilani H, Tornaritis M, Veidebaum T, and Russo P examined the association of infant feeding patterns with taste preferences in European children and adolescents. Their findings were published in Nutrients in 2019. 59. Ejlerskov KT, Christensen LB, Ritz C, Jensen SM, Mølgaard C, and Michaelsen KF studied the impact of early growth patterns and infant feeding on body composition at 3 years of age. Their findings were published in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 60. Lande B, Andersen LF, Henriksen T, Bærug A, Johansson L, and Trygg KU examined the relationships between high ponderal index at birth, feeding practices, and body mass index in infancy. Their findings were published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2005. 61. Layte R, Bennett A, McCrory C, and Kearney J studied social class variation in the predictors of rapid growth in infancy and obesity at age 3 years. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Obesity in 2014. 62. De Beer M, Vrijkotte TGM, Fall CHD, Van Eijsden M, Osmond C, and Gemke RJBJ examined associations of infant feeding and timing of linear growth and relative weight gain during early life with childhood body composition. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Obesity in 2015. 63. Zhou L, He G, Zhang J, Xie R, Walker M, and Wen SW studied risk factors for obesity in preschool children in an urban area in China. Their findings were published in the European Journal of Pediatrics in 2011. 64. Zheng M, Laws R, and Campbell KJ examined early infant feeding and body mass index trajectory in the first five years of life. Their findings were published in Obesity Research and Clinical Practice in 2019. 65. Simondon KB and Simondon F studied the age at introduction of complementary food and physical growth from 2 to 9 months in rural Senegal. Their findings were published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1997. 66. Nirmolia N, Mahanta TG, Boruah M, Rasaily R, Kotoky RP, and Bora R examined the prevalence and risk factors of pneumonia in under-five children living in slums of Dibrugarh town. Their findings were published in Clinical Epidemiology and Global Health in 2018. 67. Modjadji P and Mashishi J studied persistent malnutrition and associated factors among children under five years attending primary health facilities. Their findings were published in the South African Journal of Clinical Nutrition.
